A (Introduction to Fields)

Words: 430 Articles: 14
2009 OurBigBook.com

A2

Words: 430 Articles: 13
A OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 125
A2 OurBigBook.com
The characteristic of a field is the least positive integer r with r1K​=0, or zero if none exists. In a finite field a positive such integer exists because the sequence 0,1K​,2⋅1K​,… must repeat.
The prime subfield is the intersection of all subfields of K, equivalently the subfield generated by 1K​. In characteristic p it is the copy of Fp​ formed by the multiples of 1K​. Every field automorphism preserves 1K​ and addition, so it fixes every element of this subfield.
Finally, once the order-n Frobenius automorphism below is established, all its n powers are distinct. Any automorphism fixes F and is determined by its value at the generator λ. That value must be a root of the degree-n minimal polynomial of λ, so there are at most n automorphisms. Hence
Aut(K)=⟨ϑ⟩≅Cn​​.
(1)

a

Words: 37 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 37
a OurBigBook.com
If the positive characteristic were composite, say r=uv with 1<u,v<r, then (u1K​)(v1K​)=0 while neither factor is zero, by minimality of r. This contradicts a field having no zero divisors. Thus the characteristic is a prime p.

b

Words: 42 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 42
b OurBigBook.com
Regard K as a vector space over its prime subfield Fp​. Since K is finite, a maximal linearly independent list terminates and is a finite basis, of some dimension n≥1. Each field element has a unique coordinate vector in Fpn​, so
∣K∣=pn​.
(2)

i

Words: 44 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 44
i OurBigBook.com
For a simple field extension, the powers 1,λ,…,λd−1 form a basis when the minimal polynomial has degree d: reduction modulo that polynomial spans the extension, and a relation of smaller degree would contradict minimality. Hence [F(λ):F]=d. The field is K, whose dimension is n, giving d=n.

ii

Words: 57 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 57
ii OurBigBook.com
Define ϑ(x)=xp for every x∈K. In characteristic p, all intermediate binomial coefficients vanish, so ϑ(x+y)=ϑ(x)+ϑ(y); multiplicativity and preservation of one are immediate. If xp=yp, then (x−y)p=0 and the field property gives x=y. Thus this field homomorphism is injective, and finiteness makes it surjective. It is therefore a field automorphism, sending λ to λp as required.

iii

Words: 72 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 72
iii OurBigBook.com
Here the iteration index is a positive integer: 1≤m<n. If ϑm(λ)=λ, then ϑm fixes F and the generator, so it fixes all of K. Every element of K would then solve Tpm−T=0. A nonzero polynomial of degree pm over a field has at most pm roots, contradicting ∣K∣=pn>pm. Thus ϑm(λ)=λ. The printed inequality alone omits positivity of m; at m=0 the claimed inequality would be false.

iv

Words: 53 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 53
iv OurBigBook.com
The multiplicative group K× has order pn−1, so Lagrange's theorem for finite groups gives xpn−1=1 for x=0. Including zero, xpn=x for every x∈K. Therefore ϑn is the identity. No positive smaller power is the identity by part (iii), so
∣ϑ∣=n​.
(3)
For n=1 this says that Frobenius itself is the identity, as it should be.

i

Words: 51 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 51
i OurBigBook.com
A group action assigns to each g∈G and x∈Ω a point g⋅x so that 1⋅x=x and (gh)⋅x=g⋅(h⋅x). The orbit of x is Gx={g⋅x:g∈G}. The action is transitive if there is exactly one orbit, equivalently any point can be carried to any other by some group element.

ii

Words: 219 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 219
ii OurBigBook.com
Let G act by left multiplication on its five left cosets of H. This gives a group homomorphism φ:G→S5​. Its kernel is the core of a subgroup, ⋂g∈G​gHg−1: an element fixes every coset precisely when all its conjugates lie in H. It is a normal subgroup contained in H, so the hypothesis forces the kernel to be trivial. Thus G embeds in S5​.
The image has order 60 and index two, hence is the kernel of a surjection S5​→C2​. All transpositions are conjugate and generate S5​, so under any such surjection they must all have the same nonidentity image. This determines the map uniquely as the sign homomorphism. Its kernel is A5​, proving G≅A5​.
To prove simplicity directly, the nonidentity conjugacy classes in A5​ have sizes 15,20,12,12. A double transposition has centralizer of order four in A5​; a three-cycle has centralizer of order three; a five-cycle has centralizer of order five, yielding the two classes of size twelve. The class sizes together with the identity account for all sixty elements. A normal subgroup must be a union of these classes containing the identity, and its order must divide sixty. None of the proper nontrivial sums of these sizes with one is a divisor of sixty. Therefore A5​, and hence G, is simple.

iii

Words: 219 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 219
iii OurBigBook.com
Choose an inscribed regular tetrahedron from one of the regular compounds of five tetrahedra in the dodecahedron, and let H be its rotational stabilizer. Its twelve tetrahedral rotations preserve the dodecahedron. Concretely, with ϕ=(1+5​)/2, use dodecahedron vertices (±1,±1,±1) together with cyclic coordinate placements of (0,±ϕ−1,±ϕ). The tetrahedron has the four cube vertices whose coordinate product is +1. Cyclic coordinate permutations and even numbers of coordinate sign changes preserve both vertex sets, have determinant +1, and give twelve distinct rotations. No other rotation can preserve this tetrahedron, because a regular tetrahedron has only twelve orientation-preserving symmetries.
Their action on its four vertices is faithful and consists exactly of the even permutations: the eight rotations through ±120∘ induce three-cycles, the three half-turns induce double transpositions, and there is the identity. Thus H≅A4​, independently of part (ii).
Finally a nonidentity element of H has order two or three. In the dodecahedron's full rotation group, all fifteen half-turns about opposite-edge axes form one conjugacy class, and all twenty third-turns about opposite-vertex axes form one conjugacy class. These geometric conjugacies follow by carrying the corresponding oriented axes to one another by rotations. A normal subgroup containing such an element must contain its whole class, which already has more than twelve elements. Hence no nonidentity normal subgroup of G is contained in H, verifying the required extra property.

(pa​)≡a(p−1)/2(modp)​.

(pa​)=(−1)s​.

(6)
For p≡1,3,5,7(mod8), respectively, this count is even, odd, odd, even. Substituting these parities into the lemma gives
(p2​)={1,−1,​p≡1,7(mod8),p≡3,5(mod8).​​

(p−2​)=(p−1​)(p2​)=(−1)(p−1)/2(p2​).
(8)
Combining this with part (iv) yields
(p−2​)={1,−1,​p≡1,3(mod8),p≡5,7(mod8).​​
(9)

vi

Words: 133 Articles: 1
C2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 133
vi OurBigBook.com
Suppose all primes congruent to 3 modulo eight are p1​,…,pr​, and put N=p1​⋯pr​, an odd integer. The integer N2+2 is odd and congruent to three modulo eight. If a prime q divides it, then N2≡−2(modq) and q∤N, since a common divisor of N and N2+2 would divide two. Thus (−2/q)=1, so part (v) forces q≡1 or 3(mod8).
If all prime factors congruent to three had even multiplicity, their product, including the factors congruent to one, would be one modulo eight. Since N2+2 is three modulo eight, at least one prime factor is congruent to three and occurs to odd multiplicity. But it is none of the pi​, since those divide N. This contradiction proves infinitely many primes are congruent to three modulo eight.

Solution
Words: 71
i OurBigBook.com
On a product of sigma-finite measure spaces, Tonelli's theorem says that a nonnegative measurable function has equal product and iterated integrals, allowing +∞.
Fubini's theorem says that if a measurable function is absolutely integrable on the product, almost every section is integrable, the integrals of sections are integrable, and both iterated integrals equal the product integral. In particular, to establish absolute integrability one can first apply Tonelli's theorem to the absolute value and show its iterated integral is finite.

ii OurBigBook.com
Both terms of each one-dimensional section are integrable by a positive scaling substitution, since f∈L1(0,∞). For fixed y>0,
∫01​g(x,y)dx=y1​(∫0y​f(t)dt−∫0ay​f(t)dt)=−y1​∫yay​f(t)dt<0.
(19)
For fixed x>0,
∫1∞​g(x,y)dy=x1​(∫x∞​f(t)dt−∫ax∞​f(t)dt)=x1​∫xax​f(t)dt>0.
(20)
The strict inequalities hold because a>1 and the measurable integrand is strictly positive on each nonempty interval. If g were integrable on the stated product domain, Fubini's theorem would make both iterated integrals finite and equal. But the first order of integration would give a strictly negative value, and the other a strictly positive value. This contradiction proves g is not integrable on that product.

Let A denote the angular integral. The polar evaluation is A/2. In Cartesian coordinates Fubini's theorem instead factors the integral as

Part (i) makes A and its complement saturated, so q−1(q(A))=A and q−1(q(X∖A))=X∖A. The quotient topology therefore makes these disjoint nonempty images open, and they cover X/R. Thus the quotient is disconnected. This proves the two spaces are connected simultaneously.

The difference map (z,w)↦z−w is continuous, and X is its preimage of the open set C∖{0}. Thus X is open in the product.
The class of (z,w) is Cz​={z}×(C∖{z}). A punctured plane is path-connected: two points can be joined by a polygonal path avoiding the deleted point. Consequently every class is connected.
The projection π is onto, since (z,z+1)∈X for every z. It is continuous as a restricted coordinate projection. If U is open in X, it is open in the product because X itself is open. For a point (z,w)∈U, the product-topology basis gives open sets V,W with (z,w)∈V×W⊆U. Then V⊆π(U). Hence π(U) is open.
The map is constant exactly on the equivalence classes, so it induces a bijection π:X/R→C. It is continuous by the defining property of the quotient topology. It is also open: for quotient-open V, π(V)=π(q−1(V)) is open. Thus
X/R≅C homeomorphically​.
(27)
The plane is connected, and the classes are connected, so part (b) now yields X is connected.

Every finite upward path has positive probability, since each upward transition probability is positive. Every state i≥1 has a positive transition probability to zero because λ/(i+1)<1. From zero one can therefore reach every state, and from any state return to zero and then reach any other. Hence the chain is irreducible.
If λ<1, state zero has a positive self-loop, so its period is one. If λ=1, that self-loop disappears, but the paths 0→1→0 and 0→1→2→0 have positive probabilities and lengths two and three. Their greatest common divisor is one. Thus zero has period one in this boundary case too; irreducibility makes the whole chain aperiodic.

Part (a) proves that every vector of node values is attained uniquely, so this square linear map is bijective. Therefore An​ is invertible. Equivalently, a kernel vector would define a polynomial of degree at most n with n+1 distinct roots and would have to vanish.

has n+2 distinct zeros, at the nodes and at x. Repeated Rolle's theorem gives a point ξ between the extreme zeros, and therefore in (a,b), where R(n+1)(ξ)=0. Since pn(n+1)​=0 and ω(n+1)=(n+1)!, one gets C=f(n+1)(ξ)/(n+1)!. Substitution gives

d OurBigBook.com
Every derivative of order n+1 of sin(2x) has absolute value at most 2n+1. The equally spaced nodes are symmetric about 1/2. Pair each node a≤1/2 with 1−a; for x∈[0,1],
∣(x−a)(x−(1−a))∣=∣(x−1/2)2−(a−1/2)2∣≤41​.
(88)
If an unpaired middle node remains, its factor satisfies ∣x−1/2∣≤1/2. Consequently the complete nodal product is at most 2−(n+1). The error formula actually gives the stronger estimate
∥f−pn​∥∞​≤(n+1)!1​≤(n+1)!2⌊(n+1)/2⌋​​.
(89)
The first bound tends to zero, proving uniform convergence on the whole interval. There is no appeal to a general claim that equispaced interpolation always converges; the derivative and symmetric-product bounds are particular to this analytic function and these nodes.

Let r=∥x∥>0. Choose c=−r if x1​≥0 and c=r if x1​<0, and set v=x−ce1​. This opposite-sign choice ensures v=0. Because c2=r2,
vTx=r2−cx1​,vTv=2(r2−cx1​).

Therefore
Hv​x=x−2vvTvvTx​=x−v=ce1​​.
(94)
The denominator is positive, including when x already lies on the first coordinate axis.

d

Words: 152 Articles: 1
P4 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 152
d OurBigBook.com
Apply successive Householder reflections supported on smaller trailing coordinate sets. At step k=1,…,n−2, let x be the entries in rows k+1,…,n of column k of the current symmetric matrix. If x=0, part (c) gives an orthogonal reflection H taking it to ce1​; if x=0, use the identity. Embed this as Qk​=diag(Ik​,H) and replace the current matrix by QkT​AQk​.
The first k columns are unchanged by right multiplication. Left multiplication turns the tail of column k into a vector supported only in row k+1. Previously treated columns have zero entries throughout this trailing coordinate set, so their zeros are preserved. Symmetry makes the matching row zeros appear as well. After the final step all entries below the first subdiagonal, and by symmetry above the first superdiagonal, vanish.
The product Q=Q1​⋯Qn−2​ is orthogonal, and
QTAQ is tridiagonal​.
(95)
Restricting each transformation to its trailing coordinates is what preserves earlier zero patterns.
